headline: Symmetry shortcut narrows the search for hidden magnetic patterns
author: Sam Jarman

paragraphs.text: November 28, 2026 report
by Sam Jarman, Phys.org
edited by Gaby Clark, reviewed by Robert Egan

In some magnetic materials, the spins of individual atoms line up in highly ordered patterns but point in directions that almost completely cancel out, leaving the material unmagnetized. The exact arrangement of these spins can strongly affect how electrons move through a material, shaping both its electrical and magnetic properties. But because a single crystal can support such a huge number of plausible spin patterns, it would be impossible to test them one at a time.

Two independent research teams have now revealed how this search could be dramatically narrowed down. One team was led by Qihang Liu at the Southern University of Science and Technology in China, and the other by Takuya Nomoto at Tokyo Metropolitan University in Japan. Using differing methods, both teams have reproduced the known spin patterns of real magnets with strikingly different crystal structures.
Both studies have been published in Physical Review X.
Impossible search

While the arrangement of atoms in a crystal can be easily worked out, its magnetic structure is far harder to pin down and usually requires specialized measurements such as neutron diffraction. Researchers usually interpret these measurements using standard symmetry methods, which work out which spin patterns fit the shape of the crystal.

However, these methods often leave key details unresolved, such as the angles between neighboring spins or whether equivalent atoms carry spins of equal strength. In recent years, physicists have shown that treating rotations of the spins separately from the symmetry of the crystal itself can reveal patterns that would be missed by conventional methods.

Building on this idea, Liu's and Nomoto's teams each questioned whether crystal symmetry could narrow the search even further. To do this, the two groups first generated manageable lists of candidate patterns, then ranked them with computer simulations in two stages. First, they compared how the spins lined up relative to each other. Then they brought in spin–orbit coupling to work out how the favored patterns were oriented within the crystal.
Two different approaches

From here, the two teams diverged in their approaches. In their study, Liu's team searched for patterns repeating over regions up to four times the size of the crystal's basic building block, without having to specify the repeat length in advance. They then reproduced the known spin patterns in three very different magnets: a straight-line arrangement in MnTe, a triangular pattern in Mn₃Sn and a fully 3D arrangement in CoNb₃S₆. In a broader test, they recovered the reported magnetic structures for 73% of 1,178 materials screened.

In their own study, Nomoto's team sped up the second stage by reusing the arrangement of electrons calculated in the first round. They found that the observed pattern came out lowest in energy in 83% of 271 cases where the repeat length was already known.

Looking ahead, the two teams now hope to run stronger tests, making predictions from crystal structures measured before magnetic order sets in—before comparing them with later diffraction measurements. If successful, their approach could ultimately open up new routes to finding materials for spin-based memory and electronics.
